newsitem.title: USA: NYNEX plans additional New York City area code.
newsitem.headline: NYNEX plans additional New York City area code.

text.p: NYNEX Corp. said Friday it plans to introduce a second area code to Manhattan, New York City, in 1998 because an increase in demand for phone numbers is squeezing capacity in the borough's signature 212 area code.
NYNEX said it plans to use 646 for the new area code in Manhattan for both residential and business customers.

In the past four years, the company said demand for 212 numbers has more than tripled due to additional telephone numbers requested and from the growing number of telephone companies offering local exchange service in competition with NYNEX.
NYNEX said it will ask the New York Public Service Commission to approve an overlay programme in which the new area code would be applied to the same geographic area served by the 212 area code.
Under this option, NYNEX said, no customers in Manhattan would have to change their current numbers or area code, though those ordering new lines would be given a new code.

Alternately, the company proposed a geographic split in which Manhattan would be divided along a physical boundary such as 42nd Street or Fifth Avenue or transferring telephone numbers in a portion of the 212 area code, such as northern Manhattan, into the 718 area code.
But NYNEX said the overlay option is the least disruptive and least expensive and would provide the longest period before the supply of telephone numbers in Manhattan would run out again.

NYNEX said it will solicit input from consumers and from other telephone companies that operate in New York. It said the Public Service Commission is expected to act by September 30, after gathering input on its own.

Rising demand for new consumer technologies and the arrival of new competitors in the phone business have given rise to an explosion in the growth of new phone lines, taxing the ability of service providers to keep pace.

In response, more than 45 new area codes have been created in the last two years in the United States, according to a spokesman at Bellcore, the industry research organisation charged with maintaining the nation's phone number and area code structure.
